evals.prompt: Every Friday at 5pm, remind me in this chat to submit my timesheet. Set it up, but do not call Helio APIs in this evaluation.
evals.expected_output: Treats this as a simple one-shot-per-week message, drafts the reminder first, picks the lowest validation tier because the output is fixed text with no external side effect, and still fires one real run rather than treating the approved wording as proof. Does not invent a backtest window or failure scenarios for an automation that reads nothing.
expectations: Recognizes the request as an automation and preserves the exact Friday 5pm schedule.
Drafts or proposes the actual reminder message before discussing creation machinery.
Picks the lowest tier from step 7 (representative only) and says why: the output is fixed text with no external side effect.
Presents the tier as a one-sentence recommendation the user can adjust, rather than a fixed test matrix.
States that one real run is still required before handover, and that the approved wording on its own is not evidence that scheduled delivery works.
Does not invent a backtest window or a no-result scenario for an automation that reads no source.
States that the automation is created disabled.
States what the user must do to turn it on; a response that never mentions enabling does not satisfy this.

evals.prompt: Every weekday at 8:30am, send me a compact digest of urgent support tickets opened in the previous 24 hours. If there are none, don't wake me. Set it up but leave it disabled; do not call APIs in this evaluation.
evals.expected_output: Writes all four unseen paths into the procedure but fires only the middle tier, and gets both inputs from real windows: the representative one by moving the read window to a past weekday, the no-result one from a window verified to be empty. Does not propose waiting for tomorrow's 8:30 run to get data.
expectations: Preserves the exact 8:30am weekday schedule and produces a representative digest before formalization.
Writes all four unseen paths into the procedure's failure and no-result section, including the source-unreachable path.
Selects the middle tier and names which scenarios it covers, giving a reason tied to this automation rather than a general rule.
Explains why the source-unreachable path is written into the procedure but not fired.
States that the representative input comes from moving the read window to a named past weekday, and rejects waiting for tomorrow's scheduled run as the way to get data.
States that the no-result input must be a window verified to be empty or a read narrowed to a quiet hour, and rules out fabricating an empty response.
Uses a disabled rehearsal and transcript inspection before recommending enablement.
States that the automation is created disabled.
States what the user must do to turn it on; a response that never mentions enabling does not satisfy this.
Describes the validation loop it would run rather than listing steps it is unable to perform; a response that predominantly frames the describe-only instruction as a limitation does not satisfy this.

evals.prompt: When Stripe sends a dispute over $5,000, email legal with the customer and charge details. Set this up for me, but only describe the work in this evaluation and do not create anything.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes a high-blast-radius signed-webhook automation, picks the top tier including a baseline run, contains the outbound email before firing anything, makes the handler's don't-fire fixtures near misses rather than obvious noise, and names in plain words what this can do unattended.
expectations: Chooses a signed Stripe webhook based on source capability and verifies the signature.
Picks the top tier (the full scenario set plus a baseline run) because the automation sends email outside the company.

Contains the side effects before firing: non-owner subscribers recorded and cleared, the legal email retargeted at itself or a scratch destination, and both restored at handover from where each was saved, the recorded subscriber list via `automation update --subscriber` and the destination via the saved procedure body.

Makes the handler's don't-fire fixtures near misses (right source, right shape, below the $5,000 threshold) rather than obviously irrelevant payloads, and covers stable fire_key idempotency, invalid signatures, and duplicate deliveries.
Separates trigger-handler evidence from the disabled automation run transcript and does not enable until both pass.
Names the blast radius at handover in one plain sentence: unattended, this emails legal with customer and charge details.
States that the automation is created disabled.
States what the user must do to turn it on; a response that never mentions enabling does not satisfy this.

evals.prompt: I drafted the procedure for a weekday 8:52am US stock report at /Users/yori/.helio/runtimes/abc/procedure-stock-report.md. Set up the automation disabled. In this evaluation, describe the exact command transport only and do not call APIs.
evals.expected_output: Treats the local markdown file as a drafting source, not as the procedure value. expectations: Preserves the exact weekday 8:52am schedule and keeps the automation disabled.
Treats the draft file's markdown contents as the source of the procedure body, rather than inventing procedure content independently of the draft.
Never passes the local .md path as the value of --procedure.
Uses a JSON argument array whose --procedure element contains the markdown body, with only the JSON path passed to heliox --args-file.

States that the returned document_id gets read back to confirm the canonical document holds the procedure body, and frames that as a storage check rather than proof the procedure reads correctly to a stranger.
States that the automation is created disabled.
States what the user must do to turn it on; a response that never mentions enabling does not satisfy this.
Describes the validation loop it would run rather than listing steps it is unable to perform; a response that predominantly frames the describe-only instruction as a limitation does not satisfy this.

evals.prompt: Create a disabled weekday executive market brief automation. The facts are objective, but tone and story selection vary between AI runs, so I want confidence it will be consistently useful. Describe the creation and evaluation loop only; do not call APIs.
evals.expected_output: Uses the approved output as the standard later runs are measured against, defines observable fact/freshness/format checks while leaving tone to human review, repeats the representative run to expose variance, fires a baseline run to find out which parts of the procedure are load-bearing, grades against what was delivered, aggregates consistency, presents outputs to the user, and revises before enablement.
expectations: Produces or proposes an approved output before formalizing the automation, and treats that approved output as the standard later runs are measured against.
Separates objective checks such as freshness, required facts, citations, and delivery shape from subjective tone and story-selection review by the user.
States that the representative scenario must be run three times because the output is assembled rather than fixed, and that the spread is what gets reported rather than the best run.
Describes a baseline run whose procedure is replaced by the user's original one-line request, and explains that its purpose is to identify which parts of the procedure are load-bearing.

Grades each run after execution against what was actually delivered, with exact output or transcript evidence, then aggregates pass rate and consistency and looks for variance, hidden fallbacks, and checks that discriminate nothing.
Shows representative outputs and the evaluation summary to the user, incorporates feedback, and repeats the loop before offering enablement.
States that the automation is created disabled.
States what the user must do to turn it on; a response that never mentions enabling does not satisfy this.
Describes the validation loop it would run rather than listing steps it is unable to perform; a response that predominantly frames the describe-only instruction as a limitation does not satisfy this.

evals.prompt: 请帮我创建并配置一个自动化任务：Every weekday at 7am, compile a summary of the pull requests merged into heliohq/helio in the last 24 hours, grouped by author, and post it to this channel. Describe the automation you would create; do not call APIs in this evaluation.
evals.expected_output: Treats the user's English instruction as the authoritative language source even though a Chinese wrapper sentence surrounds it, and writes the automation name, description, and procedure entirely in English. This pins the original bug: an English instruction entering through the automation hand-off must yield English artifacts, not Chinese ones inherited from the wrapper text.
expectations: Treats the user's English instruction, not the surrounding Chinese wrapper sentence, as the authoritative language source. The wrapper text must not set the artifact language.
Writes the automation name in English.
Writes the automation description in English.
Writes the procedure document in English.
Preserves the exact weekday 7am schedule.
Procedure pins a bounded, cadence-derived read window (no unbounded read)

evals.prompt: The conversation so far has been in English. The user now writes: '每个工作日下午6点，把当天在客服频道里没有得到回复的问题整理成一份清单发给我。' Set up the automation; describe it only, do not call APIs in this evaluation.
evals.expected_output: Uses the Chinese instruction as the authoritative language source even though the room language is English: the automation name, description, and procedure are written in Chinese, while conversational replies to the user stay in the room language (English). Artifact language follows the instruction, not the room.
expectations: Uses the Chinese instruction as the authoritative language source even though the room language is English.
Writes the automation name, description, and procedure in Chinese.
Does not fall back to the room language, because the instruction is long enough to determine its language.
Keeps conversational replies to the user in the room language (English) while the artifacts stay Chinese.
Preserves the exact weekday 6pm schedule.
Procedure includes an explicit failure path distinct from the quiet no-result path

evals.prompt: Every Monday at 9am, 汇总 the previous week's 新增用户 and churn numbers, then post a short executive summary to the growth channel. Describe the automation only; do not call APIs in this evaluation.
evals.expected_output: Judges the mixed-language instruction to be dominantly English — English sentence structure and the majority of the content, with only a few embedded Chinese nouns — and therefore writes the name, description, and procedure in English (the decided dominant language) as one coherent language, not a split across two.
expectations: Judges the dominant language of the mixed instruction to be English.
Writes the automation name, description, and procedure in English, the decided dominant language.
Does not split the artifacts across two languages.
Treats the embedded Chinese nouns as vocabulary within an otherwise English artifact, not as a signal to switch the artifact's language.
Procedure pins the read window to one cadence period (previous week), not an unbounded read

evals.prompt: Earlier in this conversation you pulled the open pull requests in heliohq/helio, grouped them by author, and dropped the drafts because I said they were noise. Pins a one-week read window derived from the Monday cadence.
States that the automation is created disabled.
States what the user must do to turn it on; a response that never mentions enabling does not satisfy this.

evals.prompt: Earlier in this conversation we built a daily 9am customer-health automation with three data sources. Before I enable it, run it once and tell me whether the output looks right. Describe the validation work only; do not call APIs in this evaluation.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes this as its own step 7 rather than refiner work, because the automation has never been delivered. Runs it manually while still disabled, inspects all three sources through the --json payload, compares against the approved output, and picks a tier that three data sources warrant rather than stopping at one run.
expectations: Recognizes this as its own step 7 rather than handing it to automation-refiner: the automation has never been delivered, so proving it is still this skill's job.
Names heliox automation run for the manual fire and heliox automation run show --transcript --json for the evidence, rather than describing the loop in generic terms.
Says the evidence must be read from the structured --json payload, because cards and attachments have no plain-text equivalent.
Requires the output from all three data sources to be accounted for, not just the ones that returned data.
Compares the run output against the approved output from step 3 rather than judging it in isolation.
States that the subscriber list must be inspected before firing and that clearing it removes every recipient except the owner, who always receives the result, so a manual run is never silent.
Picks a tier that three data sources warrant, including the partial-source scenario, rather than stopping at one representative run.
States what the user must do to turn it on; a response that never mentions enabling does not satisfy this.
Describes the validation loop it would run rather than listing steps it is unable to perform; a response that predominantly frames the describe-only instruction as a limitation does not satisfy this.
